uncited: Blocky meshing is a family of surface extraction methods that convert discrete volumetric data (voxels) into polygonal meshes by treating each voxel as a primitive unit, typically a cube or a set of its faces.

Unlike smooth surface extraction methods like [Isosurface extraction](30-isosurface-extraction.md) which interpolate values to create curved surfaces, blocky meshing preserves the discrete, axis-aligned nature of the input data, resulting in "blocky" geometry.

The family is distinguished by its focus on optimizing the rendering of these discrete primitives through techniques such as face culling, greedy merging of coplanar faces, and GPU-driven classification, rather than topological smoothing.
All methods in this family operate on a discrete grid $V$ where each cell $(x,y,z)$ has an occupancy state (e.g., solid/empty) or a material ID.
The core geometric primitive is the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of the voxel.
**Discrete Representation**: The volume is represented as a 3D array.
Unlike [Isosurface extraction](30-isosurface-extraction.md), no interpolation of scalar fields is performed to determine surface position; the surface lies exactly on the voxel boundaries.
**Face-Based Extraction**: The primary geometric output is the set of exposed faces of the voxels.
A face is exposed if the adjacent voxel in the normal direction is empty (or has a different material ID, depending on the method).
**Axis-Aligned Normals**: All generated faces have normals aligned with the principal axes: $\pm \hat{x}, \pm \hat{y}, \pm \hat{z}$.
This simplifies shading and culling logic compared to arbitrary normals in smooth meshing.
**Culling**: A fundamental optimization is the removal of internal faces.
If two adjacent voxels are both solid (and treated as the same material), the shared face is not rendered.
This reduces the primitive count from $6N$ (for $N$ voxels) to approximately $2N$ for dense volumes.

Blocky meshing originates from the early days of voxel-based video games and 3D modeling, where computational resources were limited and discrete data structures were natural for terrain and world representation.
